rv.q: And then we meet Jay Gatsby (Jamie Muscato) and boy, are we rolling. Muscato, by now a West End favourite, is an inspired choice to play Gatsby, the jaded and mysterious millionaire. In this show, he is a star, bringing a rare cinematic coolness to the stage, an ability to project emotion without overacting and excessive gesturing.

But while the musical adaptation of F. Scott Fitzgerald's great American novel about money and class looks like a million dollars, the creators still struggle to overcome the essential problem of the work: none of the leading characters are likeable, not even narrator Nick Carraway (Corbin Bleu), who may not be nasty or vapid but is still (whisp...
In performance this Gatsby turns out to be a sleek, ravishingly designed ocean liner of a show, with enough musical oomph and vocal power to distract you from the hollowness at its heart.
Settle in for many exclamations of “old sport” during this centenary year, starting with this new musical, which is also currently playing on Broadway.

It is a given that Fitzgerald’s extraordinary prose will have to be truncated or coarsened. Yet when Carraway (an endearing Corbin Bleu) introduces himself at the start, before giving way to a gilded chorus proclaiming, “The Great War has been won/ The bacchanalia has begun,” you do wonder if you are in for a Simpsons-style parody of musical the...

Jon Robyns’s Tom Buchanan emanates a persuasively smooth blank cruelty but Frances Mayli McCann’s Daisy – who symbolises above all the blithely rotten heart of this gilded world – is reduced to a stock dull socialite.

There are two kinds of Great Gatsby fans. Scott Fitzgerald’s tale as an exquisite meditation on the Jazz Age version of the American Dream. The others are more interested in dressing up in fancy threads and quaffing champagne at retro parties.

There is a strong argument for turning F Scott Fitzgerald’s jazz-age critique of the American Dream into a musical, from the sound of the lavish parties at Jay Gatsby’s mansion to the natural lyricism in its prose. It does not transpose convincingly here, though not for the lack of size or volume.

When F Scott Fitzgerald’s third novel THE GREAT GATSBY was published in 1925, it was generally considered to be a weaker effort than his earlier works This Side of Paradise and The Beautiful and Damned.
Broadway star and High School Musical alumnus Corbin Bleu makes a delightful, heartfelt West End debut in what is really the leading role: narrator, and Daisy’s impecunious cousin, Nick Carraway.
